summary:
Consensual same-sex sexual conduct between adults is legal in Botswana. The High Court declared Penal Code Section 164 unconstitutional in a unanimous ruling on 11 June 2019 in Letsweletse Motshidiemang v Attorney General. The Government appealed in July 2019. The Court of Appeal unanimously rejected the appeal on 29 November 2021, holding that such laws incentivise law enforcement agents to become key-hole peepers and intruders into the private space of citizens. Paragraphs (a) and (c) of Section 164 were formally deleted from the statute book in March 2026 by the Rectification of the Laws (Penal Code) Order, 2026 under the Revision of the Laws Act after years of legislative inaction.

Before June 2019, Section 164(a) and (c) criminalised sodomy, whether heterosexual or homosexual, under a provision that applied to both men and women and carried up to seven years imprisonment. Prosecution was rare. The United States State Department 2011 Human Rights Report found police did not target same-sex activity that year. Former President Festus Mogae told the BBC he had instructed police not to arrest or harass gay people during his ten years in office, while declining to change a law he said would lose him an election.

A separate provision, Penal Code Section 167 concerning same-sex conduct between women, remained a point of contention after the 2019 ruling. At the United Nations Universal Periodic Review outcome in the 43rd session in May 2023, Botswana did not accept Canada's recommendations to repeal Section 167 and to introduce an administrative process for legal gender recognition. The review recorded that a clear administrative process for recognition was yet to be introduced.

Transgender persons in Botswana have a constitutional right to change their legal gender established through court orders rather than a routine administrative procedure. In September 2017 the High Court held that refusal by the Registrar of National Registration to change a transgender man's gender marker from female to male was unreasonable and violated constitutional rights to dignity, privacy, freedom of expression, equal protection of the law, freedom from discrimination and freedom from inhumane and degrading treatment. The Government initially announced it would appeal but decided against it in December and supplied the man with a new identity document reflecting his gender identity. In a parallel case decided in December 2017, transgender woman and activist Tshepo Ricki Kgositau won recognition of her female identity after a four-year legal battle following gender confirmation surgery in December 2016. She dedicated the victory to every single trans diverse person in Botswana. The Southern Africa Litigation Centre in May 2024 assessed that implementation of these precedents in Botswana and Namibia has not been satisfactory so far.

Same-sex couples have no legal recognition in Botswana in the form of marriage or civil unions.

In June 2019 the High Court ruled that sex in Section 3 of the Constitution must be generously and purposively interpreted to include sexual orientation. Legal commentator Carmel Rickard assessed that this gives LGBTQ Batswana an even stronger, constitutionally-based argument against discrimination.

The record on violence and social attitudes is mixed. The United States State Department 2011 report recorded no reports of violence against persons based on sexual orientation or gender identity during that year, while also documenting societal discrimination against LGBT people. Afrobarometer survey data recorded an increase from 43 percent in 2016 to 50 percent in 2021 in respondents who said they welcomed or would not be bothered by a homosexual neighbour.

Official statements reflect both hostility and protection. In February 2011 the Deputy Speaker of the National Assembly said he would have those who practise homosexuality killed if he had the power. In September 2016 President Ian Khama deported American anti-gay pastor Steven Anderson, stating that Botswana does not want hate speech in the country. In November 2018 President Mokgweetsi Masisi acknowledged that people in same-sex relationships have been violated and have also suffered in silence for fear of being discriminated against and said they deserved protection. LEGABIBO and activists described the Government's 2019 appeal against decriminalisation as an affirmation of persistent homophobia and transphobia.

A functioning, legally registered community infrastructure exists. The Court of Appeal in 2016 ordered registration of LEGABIBO on grounds of freedom of association, expression and assembly. LEGABIBO, the principal LGBTIQ+ organisation in Botswana, conducts advocacy, awareness campaigns and sexual-health and HIV work, including commemoration of World AIDS Day 2017 in Bobonong, and maintains Coming Out, Law and Constitution and Help and Support resources.
tangentialFactors:
The constitutional challenge that led to decriminalisation concerned a historic-era carnal knowledge law. Human Rights Watch in January 2018 noted the hearing was set for March 2018. The law was struck down on 11 June 2019 and the trans legal-gender right was confirmed through cases in 2017 to 2022.

A draft constitutional amendment discussed in June 2024 would add express protection from discrimination for intersex persons and people with disabilities. During deliberations that month the Minister of Labour and Home Affairs told legislators to keep intersex and same-sex distinct. Civic groups have criticised the wider constitutional review process. The intersex provision signals momentum toward broader LGBTQI+ protection.
localsOnly: The Employment Act 1982 has prohibited employment discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation since 2010.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved on the sources is whether Penal Code Section 167 retains any practical enforcement effect after the invalidation and formal deletion of Section 164(a) and (c). The inventory establishes only that a recommendation to repeal Section 167 was not accepted at the 2023 Universal Periodic Review.

Not sourced in the inventory are the current practical steps, timelines, costs or documentary requirements for a transgender resident seeking a gender-marker change by court order, beyond the fact that no clear administrative process had been introduced by May 2023.
